claim: A receiver needs at least four pseudo-ranges: three for its position and one for its clock. The geometry of the satellites (the DOP) sets how range errors grow into position errors.
The GPS nominal constellation: 24 satellites in six orbital planes, about 20 200 km high, inclined 55°, one orbit in about 12 hours.
The model spaces the 24 satellites evenly (a Walker 24/6/1 pattern); the real slots are not evenly spaced.
note: A simplification the page keeps; it changes the geometry, not the principles.

claim: The model flies the nominal 24 satellites; the operational GPS constellation has more (about 31 in recent years). With GPS alone, gaps in RAIM coverage are therefore more frequent in the model than in reality, so each scenario starts its constellation where its approach has typical geometry: RAIM supports LNAV, as it does on almost every real approach.
note: Modelling the operational constellation would be more faithful; it would change the recorded AirNav Indonesia results (tests/golden).

claim: The model lets every GPS satellite broadcast L5; not every GPS satellite does today.
GPS civil signals: L1 at 1575.42 MHz and L5 at 1176.45 MHz; all GPS satellites share each frequency (CDMA).
The speed of light is 299 792 458 m/s (exact, by definition of the metre).
WGS-84: semi-major axis 6 378 137.0 m, flattening 1/298.257223563.
The Earth rotates at 7.292115 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s (WGS-84; IS-GPS-200 uses 7.2921151467 × 10⁻⁵ rad/s). The model uses the WGS-84 value; which the orbits should use is to confirm.
sources: NIMA (now NGA) TR8350.2; US Space Force IS-GPS-200

claim: The Earth’s gravitational constant used for GPS orbits: 3.986005 × 10¹⁴ m³/s².

A range is wrong because of the satellite clock, the orbit, the ionosphere (usually the largest), the troposphere, multipath and receiver noise. SBAS corrects the first three for its region; the receiver models the troposphere; multipath and noise stay.
Illustrative 1σ sizes of the GPS broadcast clock (1.1 m) and orbit (0.8 m) errors along the line of sight.
The receiver’s tropospheric model: mapping m(E) = 1.001 / √(0.002001 + sin²E), residual σ of 0.12 m at the zenith.
Airborne multipath σ = 0.13 + 0.53·e^(−θ/10°) m and receiver noise σ = 0.36 m (an AAD-A-like receiver).
Reference stations at surveyed positions over a large area monitor the satellites and send their data to master stations.
Master stations compute clock and orbit corrections for each satellite and ionospheric delays on a grid, and bound what is left.
UDRE bounds the residual clock and orbit error of each satellite; GIVE bounds the error of each grid point’s ionospheric delay.
"Do Not Use" and "Not Monitored" satellites cannot be used with SBAS integrity; LP and LPV also need UDREI other than 13.
value: 13, 14, 15 UDREI (not for LPV, Not Monitored, Do Not Use)

claim: The UDREI table: UDRE 0.75, 1.0, 1.25, 1.75, 2.25, 3.0, 3.75, 4.5, 5.25, 6.0, 7.5, 15, 50 and 150 m for UDREI 0–13; 14 is Not Monitored and 15 Do Not Use.
sources: RTCA DO-229 Table A-6; ICAO Annex 10 Appendix B

claim: σ_UDRE is taken as UDRE / 3.29 (UDRE bounds 99.9 %); DO-229 tabulates σ²_UDRE for each UDREI, and the two agree to the table’s rounding (UDREI 0: 0.0520 m²).
σ_GIVE is taken as GIVE / 3.29; DO-229 tabulates σ²_GIVE for each GIVEI (GIVEI 0: 0.0084 m²).
Ionospheric grid points are 5° apart in latitude and longitude between 55°S and 55°N.
The ionosphere is modelled as a thin shell 350 km above the Earth; pierce points and the obliquity factor follow from it.
Uplink stations send the messages to the SBAS GEO satellites, which rebroadcast them; a GEO stays over the equator at a fixed longitude.
An SBAS GEO broadcasts one 250-bit message every second (250 bit/s, 500 symbols/s after forward error correction). On L1 a message is an 8-bit preamble, a 6-bit type, 212 data bits and a 24-bit CRC.
sources: ICAO Annex 10 Appendix B; RTCA DO-229
note: The recorded EGNOS messages (src/replay) confirm the L1 layout: every one passes the 24-bit CRC over this layout and starts with an 8-bit preamble.

claim: A DFMC message on L5 is also 250 bits a second, but with a 4-bit preamble: 4 + 6 + 216 + 24 bits.
sources: EUROCAE ED-259; ICAO Annex 10 DFMC SBAS SARPs
note: The 4-bit preamble is confirmed by public summaries of the DFMC SARPs; 216 data bits follow from the 250-bit total.

With satellite status and clock and orbit corrections, SBAS supports departure to non-precision approach; with the ionospheric grid too, approaches with vertical guidance up to Category I.
The receiver combines UDRE, GIVE and its own error models into protection levels (HPL, VPL) and compares them with the alert limits (HAL, VAL).
HPL = K_H·d_major and VPL = K_V·d_V, with K_H = 6.0 for approaches with vertical guidance and 6.18 otherwise, and K_V = 5.33.
sources: RTCA DO-229 Appendix J; ICAO Annex 10 Appendix B

claim: GPS alone uses RAIM/FDE; its detection thresholds and protection-level factors are illustrative values (false-alarm probability about 10⁻⁵).
Satellites below 5° elevation are not tracked, by the aircraft or by the reference stations.
GPS alone: the σ of the broadcast-model ionospheric residual is taken as 9 m vertically at low magnetic latitudes, times the obliquity.
The DFMC service’s correction bound (DFRE) is modelled with the same bound as UDRE; the DFREI table of ED-259 differs.
The avionics annunciate the highest level of service the signal supports: LPV, LNAV/VNAV or LNAV.
The final approach segment (FAS) data block defines the LPV final approach, and a CRC protects it.

The FAS data block’s fields (operation type, provider, airport, runway, performance designator, reference path, threshold, glide path, threshold crossing height, course width, HAL, VAL), with a typical 105 m course width at the threshold.
sources: RTCA DO-229; ICAO Annex 10 Appendix B

claim: The FAS data block CRC is a 32-bit CRC (CRC-32Q, polynomial 0x814141AB).
note: The CRC of the single byte 0x01 is the polynomial itself, which is how the binding reads it.

The decision height of each scenario’s LPV procedure is illustrative: 250 ft at Bali, 200 ft for the LPV-200 at Nice.
LNAV/VNAV, LP and LPV need the avionics to track two SBAS satellites.

The time to alert is the longest time allowed from a fault to the alert in the cockpit.
ADS-B broadcasts the GNSS position; its integrity, linked to the GNSS alert limits, lets the controller trust the position on the screen.
States verify SBAS performance and issue NOTAMs for degradations, using a service volume model.
On loss of GNSS: inertial systems, DME, VOR/DME, ILS and procedural control by ATC.

With GPS alone (ABAS) approaches go down to LNAV minima; there is no vertical protection level.

Radiotelephony for GNSS problems, as PANS-ATM gives it: a controller warns "GNSS REPORTED UNRELIABLE" (or "GNSS MAY NOT BE AVAILABLE [DUE TO INTERFERENCE]"); a crew that cannot fly an RNP procedure reports "UNABLE RNP".

claim: The ionospheric delay follows the sun; storms make the ionosphere thicker and less even.
Near the magnetic equator, dense bands about 15° either side and post-sunset bubbles make single-frequency SBAS vertical guidance (APV, Category I) impractical.
Severe scintillation is common near the equator after sunset; it is patchy, takes out a few satellites at a time and affects every frequency.
The dual-frequency ionosphere-free combination removes the (first-order) ionospheric delay but amplifies noise and multipath by about 2.6.
The GPS broadcast ionospheric model removes about half of the delay; SBAS reduces the error to a few metres and bounds it.
The sizes of the ionospheric threat terms (the daytime band margin, the post-sunset threat, the storm) are illustrative, chosen to reproduce Doc 9849’s conclusions qualitatively.
The magnetic (dip) equator is read approximately from IGRF maps every 15° of longitude (about 9–10°N over Indonesia).
Dual-frequency multi-constellation (DFMC) SBAS services are planned, not yet operational (WAAS about 2026, EGNOS from 2028).
Dual-frequency SBAS makes approaches with vertical guidance possible in equatorial States.
